items.title: eBPF Rootkits: Why Underground Actors Are Taking Notice
items.summary: Linux eBPF rootkits can hide malicious activity and evade traditional detection methods without loading kernel modules. Flare reveals how these techniques are spreading through underground forums, where threat actors are sharing rootkit source code, tutorials, and exploits target
items.content:
eBPF Rootkits: Why Underground Actors Are Taking Notice

For years, eBPF (extended Berkeley Packet Filter) has been one of the most celebrated technologies in the Linux kernel. It lets developers run sandboxed programs inside the kernel without writing kernel modules, while powering everything from network monitoring to security tooling.

Linux is extremely popular in production servers and giants like Google, Cloudflare, and Meta rely on it daily.

The same eBPF capabilities that are attractive for defenders, however, can be a powerful weapon in the hands of attackers. Flare’s research found underground forum posts sharing eBPF rootkit code and step-by-step tutorials.

One Russian-language post described how to build an implant with process hiding and packet-triggered activation, and included screenshots the author presented as demonstrations.

Traditional Linux rootkits typically rely on loadable kernel modules (LKMs) to hook system calls and hide malicious activity. These are well-understood by defenders, and most EDR solutions watch for suspicious module loads. eBPF, however, behaves in a different way.

An eBPF malware can hook into kernel functions, observe system calls, or inspect and modify network traffic using the same kernel-supported bpf() interface as legitimate tools like Cilium.

Its programs run without loading a kernel module, so a routine lsmod check can miss them. The challenge for defenders is determining who loaded the program and what it does.

The Next Linux Rootkit Is Already Being Discussed Underground

eBPF rootkits are moving from conference talks to underground forum tutorials, and by the time one loads on a host, it’s built to evade your usual checks.

Flare monitors forums, marketplaces, and paste sites in real time, so your team sees new tooling, exploits, and chatter early enough to track eBPF threats.

From Classic BPF Backdoors to eBPF Rootkits

The first major wake-up call came in 2022 when PwC and Elastic Security Labs documented BPFDoor, a passive Linux backdoor attributed to a Chinese threat actor tracked as Red Menshen. The BPFDoor sample Elastic analyzed used a classic BPF socket filter to recognize specially crafted TCP, UDP, or ICMP packets.

Once triggered, it could open a reverse shell or redirect traffic to the implant. PwC discovered the malware in 2021, and public reporting in 2022 described activity targeting organizations in the Middle East and Asia.

Around the same time, Intezer and BlackBerry jointly disclosed Symbiote, a different flavor of Linux malware that weaponizes BPF for stealth. Rather than running as a standalone process, Symbiote uses the dynamic linker to preload a malicious shared library into affected processes.

The library intercepts calls to setsockopt() that attach classic BPF filters via SO_ATTACH_FILTER and prepends its own filter instructions to conceal selected traffic from packet capture.

Public research had already demonstrated offensive uses of eBPF. In 2021, researchers presented ebpfkit at Black Hat USA and DEF CON. TripleCross combines syscall hooks with XDP and traffic control programs to support library injection, execution hijacking, concealment, and command and control.

Boopkit uses getdents64 hooks to hide directory entries. An already installed implant can be triggered remotely in two documented ways, one involving a malformed TCP SYN and the other using ordinary TCP connections.

Lastly, in October 2025, Synacktiv reported LinkPro after investigating a compromise that began with an exposed Jenkins server. LinkPro used eBPF programs to hide activity on the host and activate the backdoor when it received a specially crafted packet.

Underground Adoption: From Research to Weaponization

items.content:
Unit 42 has identified Falcon (aka XG or Xiàng Gē), which is a command and control (C2) framework that compromises victims' browsers by running malicious JavaScript. An actor leveraged Falcon to compromise visitors of webmail portals and government web applications by placing malicious JavaScript directly within these sites.

Operating entirely inside the browser context, attackers have used the framework to sideload malicious Chrome extensions and steal the following information:

Falcon also served as a delivery mechanism for an implant we call Antino, which uses Microsoft OneDrive as a C2 channel.

Our analysis identified the compromise of government entities in one Middle Eastern country and four Southeast Asian countries between March and May 2026. The campaigns we observed targeted ministries of foreign affairs, defense and interior, and law enforcement agencies, consistent with strategic intelligence collection objectives.

Palo Alto Networks customers are better protected from the threats discussed in this article through the following products and services:

Organizations can access tailored adversary intelligence, direct analyst consultations, and specialized exposure tracking through Unit 42 Threat Intel Services and its Deep and Dark Web Service .

If you think you might have been compromised or have an urgent matter, contact the Unit 42 Incident Response team .

Falcon C2 management panels are designed to remain semi-hidden. When accessed, the panel displays a blank page with no visible branding or login interface.

To deter casual inspection, the page disables the right-click context menu via a global contextmenu listener that calls preventDefault() . The login form also stays hidden until the F9 key is pressed three consecutive times; any other keystroke resets the counter.

Figure 1 below shows the JavaScript code for this key tracking.

Once triggered, the page displays a branded Falcon panel featuring a stylized bird logo and credential input fields. This operational security (OPSEC) mechanism ensures that it does not directly expose the login page to bots, unintended visitors and automated systems that grab webpage screenshots.

Figure 2 below shows a screenshot of the login panel.

Falcon is written in NodeJS and has two listeners. One listener is for the management panel interface on TCP port 8080 and the victim-facing listener is on TCP port 443.

On the victim-facing listener, we observed a JavaScript-based version of the classic game Tetris serving as the default page, designed to blend in further. Another instance hosted a game of Snake. Figure 3 below shows both versions.

In January 2026, Trend Micro reported on a scripting framework dubbed PeckBirdy . They described it as a versatile tool for exploiting living-off-the-land (LotL) binaries (LOLBins).

Our comparison with PeckBirdy revealed that it shares near-identical URL structures, payload delivery mechanisms and communication protocols with Falcon. Table 1 compares the URL structures of the two frameworks.

Table 1. URL structure comparison between Falcon and PeckBirdy.

Both frameworks use the same payload delivery sequence to execute HTA, HTML or JScript payloads, with the primary distinction being Falcon's inclusion of the /config/ path prefix.Both frameworks use AES for data encryption. PeckBirdy relies solely on AES with a predetermined encryption key, whereas Falcon negotiates an AES session key with the server, encrypted with RSA.Most significantly, both frameworks store their persistent session ID using the same Baidu-mimicking naming convention:

Based on these extensive technical overlaps, we assess with high confidence that Falcon and PeckBirdy represent variants of the same core framework.

items.content:
Threat actors have been observed targeting Qlik Sense servers to unsuccessfully deliver PowerShell reverse shell commands against multiple environments in October 2026.

Cynet's CyOps and Research teams said they identified the suspicious activity in October 2026 against several E.U.-based customers within a narrow window of just over three minutes.

The activity has been found to share some level of overlap with a November 2023 campaign documented by Arctic Wolf in which threat actors linked to the CACTUS ransomware operation likely weaponized then-newly-disclosed flaws in Qlik Sense to obtain initial access to target environments.

The vulnerabilities in question, which were patched by Qlik Sense in August and September 2023, impact Qlik Sense Enterprise for Windows -

It's worth noting that CVE-2023-48365 (aka DoubleQlik) is an incomplete fix for CVE-2023-41265.

In November 2023 CACTUS ransomware campaign, threat actors were observed exploiting the flaws to establish a foothold and download additional payloads to establish persistence and remote control by deploying ManageEngine Unified Endpoint Management and Security (UEMS), AnyDesk, and Plink.

The latest activity detected by Cynet involves the use of a PowerShell command containing a one-line reverse shell that connects to " 45.115.26[.]23 " on port 4455. The exact vulnerability exploited to break into Qlik Sense servers is currently not known.

"The command was executed under scheduler.exe, resembling the 2023 Cactus Qlik intrusions," the cybersecurity company said.

Although attempts to spawn the reverse shell were blocked, Cynet's testing of the reverse shell in a controlled environment has revealed that the interactive communication channel is used to conduct reconnaissance and deliver a PowerShell script for enabling persistence.

This is achieved by means of a Windows Go reverse shell that connects to "45.115.26[.]23:4456." The backdoor is then used to look for actively running processes related to Apache ActiveMQ. On Linux, the malware also attempts to collect system information and read "/etc/shadow" and "/etc/passwd" files.

A second variant of the PowerShell script attempts to install OpenSSH and creates a scheduled task named "WinUpdCheck" that launches a PowerShell reverse shell written to "C:\ProgramData\ssh\winc.ps1" at five-minute intervals.

"If sshd remained unavailable, it downloaded OpenSSH-Win64.zip from the staging server, extracted it, and ran install-sshd.ps1," Cynet said. "It set sshd to automatic startup, started the service, and added an inbound firewall rule for TCP 22. The archive was a legitimate OpenSSH package reused by the operator."

Further analysis of the infrastructure has uncovered an exposed directory ("45.115.26[.]23:8012") consisting of a custom Go backdoor for Windows, SSH persistence scripts, an ActiveMQ exploit for CVE-2023-46604 , and a modified public Veeam toolchain for CVE-2024-40711 , indicating the threat actor is possibly laying the groundwork for broader attacks.

items.content:
Asus and Zoom are among the tech companies that have released fresh security updates for their products this week.

Computer maker Asus published an advisory describing four high- and medium-severity vulnerabilities in certain router firmware releases.

Successful exploitation of the flaws could allow attackers to execute arbitrary commands with root privileges or overwrite memory and cause a crash.

Zoom has patched two vulnerabilities in Workplace for Windows, including a critical-severity unauthenticated privilege escalation bug tracked as CVE-2026-108186 (CVSS score of 9.6).

The second issue (CVE-2026-108187, CVSS score of 8.1) could also allow remote, unauthenticated attackers to elevate their privileges.

Zoom Workplace for Windows versions 7.1.8 and later contain patches for both bugs. Zoom makes no mention of any of these flaws being exploited in the wild. Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

Additionally, Cisco updated several advisories: it added fresh information on Node2Shell ’s impact and on an authorization bypass’s impact on ISE and ISE-PIC, and added new details on the availability of fixes for seven critical- and high-severity CVEs in Meraki products.

On Tuesday, both Cisco and SonicWall announced they have removed root certificates affected by compromised eMudhra intermediate certificates .

The fresh security updates arrived among hundreds of patches from Apple , Fortinet , Citrix, Ivanti , Intel, AMD , Microsoft , Adobe , SAP , and multiple ICS vendors .
